notes:
1. Government Revenue — Meaning and Importance

  • Government revenue refers to income received by the government from different sources to finance public expenditure.
  • It supports administration, development, economic management and welfare functions.
  • Revenue finances areas such as education, health care, defence, infrastructure, agriculture, rural development, public safety and social welfare.

2. Government Revenue — Union, State and Local Levels

  • Union, State and Local Governments have different revenue sources.
  • These differences arise from India's constitutional and fiscal structure.
  • A stable and predictable revenue system helps governments provide public services continuously.

3. Government Revenue — Economic Role

Government revenue influences:

  • Economic growth.
  • Income distribution.
  • Resource allocation.
  • Public investment.
  • Macroeconomic stability.

4. Government Receipts — Basic Classification

  • Government receipts include all money received by the government during a financial year.
  • Government receipts are broader than revenue receipts.

They are broadly classified into:

  • Revenue receipts.
  • Capital receipts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Total Government Receipts = Revenue Receipts + Capital Receipts

5. Revenue Receipts — Meaning

  • Revenue receipts generally do not create a liability for the government.
  • They generally do not reduce government assets.

Examples include:

  • Tax revenue.
  • Fees.
  • Interest receipts.
  • Dividends.
  • Certain grants.
📌 Must-Memorise

Revenue Receipt → No Liability + No Reduction of Assets

6. Capital Receipts — Meaning

  • Capital receipts either create liabilities or reduce government assets.

Major examples include:

  • Borrowings.
  • Recovery of loans.
  • Disinvestment proceeds.
📌 Must-Memorise

Capital Receipt → Creates Liability or Reduces Asset

7. Borrowing — Why It Is Not Revenue

  • Borrowing provides resources to the government.
  • It creates a future repayment liability.
  • It is therefore classified as a capital receipt rather than ordinary revenue.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Borrowing → Government Receipt

Borrowing ≠ Revenue Receipt

8. Revenue Receipts — Tax and Non-Tax Revenue

Revenue receipts are broadly divided into:

  • Tax revenue.
  • Non-tax revenue.
📌 Must-Memorise

Revenue Receipts = Tax Revenue + Non-Tax Revenue

9. Tax Revenue — Meaning

  • Tax revenue consists of compulsory payments imposed by government under law.
  • Taxes are collected to finance collective public purposes.
  • A taxpayer does not receive a specific equal-value service in return for each tax payment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tax → Compulsory Payment under Law

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tax ≠ Direct Payment for a Specific Service

10. Non-Tax Revenue — Meaning and Sources

  • Non-tax revenue means government income from sources other than taxation.

Important sources include:

  • Interest receipts.
  • Dividends.
  • Profits.
  • Fees.
  • Royalties.
  • Licence charges.
  • User charges.
📌 Must-Memorise

Non-Tax Revenue → Interest + Dividends + Fees + Royalties + Charges

11. Direct Tax — Meaning

  • A direct tax is imposed directly on income, profit, property or similar taxable capacity.
  • Its legal burden is generally intended to remain on the person or entity taxed.
  • Direct taxation is commonly associated with the ability-to-pay principle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Direct Tax → Burden Generally Remains on Taxpayer

12. Major Direct Taxes

Important direct taxes include:

  • Income tax.
  • Corporation tax.
📌 Must-Memorise

Income Tax + Corporation Tax → Direct Taxes

13. Income Tax

  • Income tax is imposed on taxable income according to applicable law.
  • Individuals and other specified taxpayers may be liable depending on income and legal status.
  • It is an important source of Union tax revenue.

14. Corporation Tax

  • Corporation tax is imposed on taxable profits of companies according to law.
  • It is an important source of Union Government tax revenue.

15. Direct Taxes — Advantages and Limitations

Advantages:

  • Can be linked to ability to pay.
  • Can promote equity.
  • Can be designed progressively.
  • Revenue can rise with income and business profits.

Limitations:

  • Complex rules can increase compliance costs.
  • Poor design may encourage avoidance.
  • Administration requires accurate reporting and strong compliance.

16. Effective Direct-Tax System — Requirements

A sound direct-tax system requires:

  • Clear laws.
  • Efficient administration.
  • Accurate reporting.
  • Strong compliance.

17. Indirect Tax — Meaning

  • An indirect tax is generally imposed on production, sale, supply or consumption of goods and services.
  • The person legally paying the tax may pass some or all of its economic burden through prices.
  • Consumers often bear the final economic burden.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indirect Tax → Burden Can Be Shifted

18. GST — Major Indirect Tax

  • GST is a major broad-based indirect tax in the Indian tax system.
  • It is a destination-based tax on the supply of goods and services.
  • It replaced several earlier Union and State indirect taxes.
📌 Must-Memorise

GST → Indirect + Destination-Based Tax

19. Customs Duty

  • Customs duties are imposed on goods entering or leaving the country according to applicable law.
  • Import duties can generate revenue.
  • They can also influence prices and competitiveness of imported goods.
📌 Must-Memorise

Customs Duty → Indirect Tax

20. Union Excise Duties

  • Union excise duties continue to apply to certain specified products treated separately from the broad GST system.
  • Exact coverage and rates can change through law and policy.

21. Indirect Taxes — Advantages and Equity Concern

Advantages:

  • Can raise substantial revenue from a broad consumption base.
  • Can be collected through businesses at different stages.
  • Can influence consumption behaviour.

Limitation:

  • They can place a relatively heavier burden on lower-income households when essential consumption is taxed similarly across income groups.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indirect Tax ≠ Always Equitable

22. Direct vs Indirect Tax

Direct tax:

  • Imposed directly on income or profit.
  • Burden generally remains on taxpayer.
  • Examples → Income tax, corporation tax.

Indirect tax:

  • Generally imposed through transactions involving goods and services.
  • Burden can be shifted through prices.
  • Examples → GST, customs duty.

23. Union Government — Major Tax Sources

Important Union tax sources include:

  • Income tax.
  • Corporation tax.
  • Union share of GST.
  • Customs duties.
  • Specified Union excise duties.
  • Cesses.
  • Surcharges.

24. Tax Collection vs Tax Sharing

  • The authority collecting a tax and the constitutional rule determining its final distribution may be different.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tax Collection ≠ Final Distribution of Tax Revenue

25. State Governments — Revenue Need

State revenue finances:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Agriculture.
  • Police.
  • State infrastructure.
  • Local development.
  • Welfare.

26. SGST — State Goods and Services Tax

  • SGST is collected by States on taxable intra-State supplies under the GST framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

SGST → State Tax on Intra-State Supply

27. State Tax Sources Outside GST

Important State sources include:

  • Taxes on specified petroleum products.
  • State excise.
  • Stamp duties.
  • Registration charges.
  • Motor vehicle taxes.
  • Certain land-related revenues.

28. State Excise

  • State excise is an important State revenue source.
  • It is particularly associated with alcoholic liquor for human consumption and other matters assigned to States.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Excise → Important State Revenue Source

29. Stamp Duty and Registration Charges

  • States receive revenue from stamp duties on specified legal instruments.
  • Registration charges on property transactions and legal instruments also provide State revenue.

30. Motor Vehicle Tax

  • State Governments levy motor vehicle taxes according to the applicable legal framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

Motor Vehicle Tax → Mainly State Revenue

31. State Tax Sources — Memory Pairings

  • SGST → State.
  • State excise → State.
  • Motor vehicle tax → State.
  • Stamp and registration revenue → State.

32. Union Non-Tax Revenue

Major Union non-tax sources include:

  • Interest receipts.
  • Dividends.
  • Profits or surplus transfers.
  • Fees.
  • Licence receipts.
  • Spectrum-related receipts.
  • Administrative and service receipts.

33. Interest, Dividends and Profits

  • Interest received by government on loans and advances is non-tax revenue.
  • Dividends received from public-sector enterprises and institutions are non-tax revenue.
  • Profits or surplus transfers from public institutions may also contribute.
📌 Must-Memorise

Interest + Dividends → Non-Tax Revenue

34. Fees, Licence and Spectrum Receipts

  • Government fees for specified services form part of non-tax revenue.
  • Licence receipts can contribute to non-tax income.
  • Spectrum-related receipts may also provide non-tax revenue where applicable.

35. Borrowing — Not Non-Tax Revenue

  • Borrowing is a capital receipt.
  • It is neither tax revenue nor non-tax revenue.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Borrowing ≠ Non-Tax Revenue

36. State Non-Tax Revenue

State non-tax revenue may arise from:

  • State-owned enterprises.
  • Interest.
  • Royalties.
  • Fees.
  • User charges.
  • Forest receipts.
  • Irrigation receipts.
  • Departmental receipts.

37. Royalty — Meaning

  • A royalty is a payment made for the right to use or extract a resource.
  • Mineral royalties can be important for resource-rich States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Royalty → Right to Use / Extract Resource

38. User Charges

  • User charges are payments collected from users of specified public services.
  • They have a more direct connection with the service received than taxes do.

Examples may relate to:

  • Transport.
  • Water.
  • Irrigation.
  • Administrative services.

39. Tax vs Fee

Tax:

  • Compulsory general contribution.
  • No direct one-to-one service relationship.

Fee:

  • Generally linked to a specific service, permission, registration or administrative activity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tax ≠ Fee

40. Fine — Meaning and Purpose

  • A fine is imposed for violation of a law, rule or regulatory requirement.
  • Its primary purpose is punishment, enforcement and deterrence rather than revenue generation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fine → Punishment / Deterrence

41. Grant — Meaning

  • A grant is a transfer of funds from one government or institution to another without an obligation to repay it as a loan.
  • Union grants can form an important resource source for States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Grant → No Repayment Obligation

42. Tax, Fee, Fine and User Charge — Core Distinction

  • Tax → Compulsory general contribution.
  • Fee → Specific service or regulatory activity.
  • Fine → Violation of law or rule.
  • User charge → Beneficiary pays for service.

43. Capital Receipts — Borrowing

  • Borrowing creates a liability because the amount has to be repaid.
  • Government may borrow for infrastructure, development programmes or temporary fiscal gaps.
  • Borrowing can occur through government securities, treasury instruments and other permitted mechanisms.
📌 Must-Memorise

Borrowing → Liability ↑ → Capital Receipt

44. Capital Receipts — Recovery of Loans

  • When government receives repayment of loans previously given, the amount is treated as a capital receipt.
  • Loan recovery reduces a financial asset of the government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Loan Recovery → Financial Asset ↓

45. Capital Receipts — Disinvestment

  • Disinvestment occurs when government reduces ownership in a public-sector enterprise or other asset.
  • The proceeds are treated as capital receipts because government ownership in an asset is reduced.
📌 Must-Memorise

Disinvestment → Government Ownership ↓

46. Capital Receipts — Core Difference

  • Borrowing → Liability increases.
  • Loan recovery → Financial asset decreases.
  • Disinvestment → Government ownership decreases.

47. Public Borrowing — Future Cost

  • Borrowing provides resources today.
  • It creates future repayment obligations.
  • It also creates future interest expenditure.
  • Excessive borrowing can raise public debt and the interest burden.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Borrowing Today → Repayment + Interest Tomorrow

48. Federal Fiscal System

  • India follows a federal fiscal system.
  • Revenue powers and expenditure responsibilities are divided between the Union and States.

49. Tax Devolution

  • Tax devolution means transfer of a constitutionally determined share of divisible Union taxes to the States.
  • The Finance Commission recommends how divisible taxes are shared between the Union and States and among States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tax Devolution → Share of Union Taxes to States

50. Finance Commission — Revenue Sharing Role

The Finance Commission recommends:

  • Distribution of divisible Union taxes between Union and States.
  • Distribution of the States' share among individual States.
  • Specified grants.

51. Vertical Devolution

  • Vertical devolution refers to distribution of divisible tax resources between the Union and all States collectively.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vertical → Union vs States

52. Horizontal Distribution

  • Horizontal distribution refers to allocation of the States' share among individual States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Horizontal → Among States

53. Vertical vs Horizontal — Core Distinction

  • Vertical → Union and States collectively.
  • Horizontal → Individual States among themselves.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Vertical ≠ Among States

Horizontal ≠ Union vs States

54. Grants-in-Aid

  • Grants-in-aid are transfers made to States under constitutional and fiscal arrangements.
  • They can help address differences between State expenditure needs and revenue capacity.

55. Cess — Meaning

  • A cess is generally a tax or levy imposed for a specified purpose.
  • Its proceeds are associated with the purpose for which it is imposed, subject to law and budgetary arrangements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cess → Specified Purpose

56. Surcharge — Meaning

  • A surcharge is an additional charge imposed on an existing tax.
📌 Must-Memorise

Surcharge → Additional Charge on Existing Tax

57. Cess vs Surcharge

  • Cess → Generally linked to a specified purpose.
  • Surcharge → Additional amount imposed over an existing tax liability.
  • Their constitutional treatment may differ from ordinary Union taxes included in the divisible pool.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cess / Surcharge ≠ Automatically Ordinary Shareable Union Tax

58. Good Tax System — Basic Principles

A good tax system should balance:

  • Revenue mobilisation.
  • Fairness.
  • Simplicity.
  • Efficiency.
  • Economic growth.

59. Equity — Principle of Taxation

  • Tax burden should be distributed fairly among taxpayers.

Horizontal equity:

  • Similar taxpayers should generally be treated similarly.

Vertical equity:

  • Those with greater ability to pay may bear a greater burden.
📌 Must-Memorise

Horizontal Equity → Similar People, Similar Treatment

Vertical Equity → Greater Ability, Greater Burden

60. Certainty, Convenience and Economy

Certainty:

  • Taxpayer should know how much, when and how tax must be paid.

Convenience:

  • Payment method and timing should be reasonably convenient.

Economy:

  • Collection cost should not be unnecessarily high compared with revenue collected.

61. Simplicity, Adequacy, Elasticity and Neutrality

Simplicity:

  • Tax laws should be understandable.

Adequacy:

  • Tax system should raise sufficient revenue.

Elasticity:

  • Revenue should be capable of rising as the economy expands.

Neutrality:

  • Taxation should avoid unnecessary distortion unless intervention is deliberate.

62. Progressive Tax

  • A progressive tax imposes a higher effective burden as taxable income increases.
  • It is closely associated with ability to pay.
📌 Must-Memorise

Progressive → Burden Rises with Income

63. Proportional Tax

  • A proportional tax applies the same tax rate across the relevant tax base.
📌 Must-Memorise

Proportional → Same Rate

64. Regressive Tax

  • A regressive tax places a relatively heavier burden on lower-income groups.
  • Some consumption taxes can have regressive effects because poorer households may spend a larger share of income on taxed consumption.
📌 Must-Memorise

Regressive → Relatively Heavier on Lower-Income Groups

65. Progressive vs Proportional vs Regressive

  • Progressive → Relative burden rises with income.
  • Proportional → Same rate.
  • Regressive → Relative burden heavier on lower incomes.

66. Tax Base and Tax Rate

Tax base:

  • Income, profit, transaction, property, consumption or activity on which tax is calculated.

Tax rate:

  • Rate or amount applied to the tax base.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tax Base → What Is Taxed

Tax Rate → Rate Applied

67. Broad Tax Base

  • A broad tax base can enable government to raise substantial revenue without relying excessively on very high tax rates.

68. Tax Buoyancy

  • Tax buoyancy measures how strongly tax revenue changes in response to changes in national income or economic output.
  • It includes the effects of discretionary tax-policy changes.
  • If tax revenue grows faster than the economy, buoyancy can exceed one.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tax Buoyancy → Includes Policy Changes

69. Tax Elasticity

  • Tax elasticity measures responsiveness of tax revenue to changes in the tax base after excluding discretionary tax-policy changes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tax Elasticity → Excludes Policy Changes

70. Tax Buoyancy vs Tax Elasticity

  • Buoyancy → Includes discretionary policy changes.
  • Elasticity → Excludes discretionary policy changes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tax Buoyancy ≠ Tax Elasticity

71. Tax Evasion

  • Tax evasion involves illegally concealing income, transactions or taxable activities to reduce tax liability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tax Evasion → Illegal

72. Tax Avoidance

  • Tax avoidance generally means arranging affairs within the wording of existing law to reduce tax liability.
  • Aggressive forms may be restricted through anti-avoidance provisions.

73. Tax Evasion vs Tax Avoidance

  • Evasion → Illegal concealment.
  • Avoidance → Uses legal arrangements, though aggressive avoidance may be restricted.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Evasion ≠ Avoidance

74. Tax Compliance

Tax compliance includes:

  • Registration.
  • Correct reporting.
  • Filing returns.
  • Paying tax according to law.
  • Better compliance can raise revenue without increasing statutory tax rates.
📌 Must-Memorise

Better Compliance → Higher Revenue Without Higher Rates

75. Digitalisation and Tax Administration

Digitalisation can improve:

  • Electronic filing.
  • Electronic payments.
  • Information reporting.
  • Data matching.
  • Transparency.
  • Detection of inconsistencies.
  • Compliance.

76. Tax-GDP Ratio

  • Tax-GDP ratio compares total tax revenue with the size of the economy.
  • It is widely used as an indicator of tax mobilisation capacity.
  • A rising ratio can provide greater fiscal space.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tax-GDP Ratio → Tax Revenue Relative to GDP

77. Tax-GDP Ratio — Important Limitation

  • A higher tax-GDP ratio alone does not prove that a tax system is fair or efficient.
  • Quality, equity and efficiency of taxation must also be considered.

78. Core Revenue Memory Chain

  • Government Receipts → Revenue + Capital.
  • Revenue Receipts → Tax + Non-Tax.
  • Capital Receipts → Borrowing + Loan Recovery + Disinvestment.

79. Direct and Indirect Tax Memory Chain

  • Income tax → Direct.
  • Corporation tax → Direct.
  • GST → Indirect.
  • Customs duty → Indirect.

80. Union Revenue Memory Chain

Union tax sources:

  • Income tax.
  • Corporation tax.
  • GST components.
  • Customs.
  • Specified excise.
  • Cesses.
  • Surcharges.

Union non-tax sources:

  • Interest.
  • Dividends.
  • Profits.
  • Fees.
  • Licence receipts.
  • Spectrum receipts.

81. State Revenue Memory Chain

State tax sources:

  • SGST.
  • State excise.
  • Motor vehicle tax.
  • Stamp duties.
  • Registration charges.

State non-tax sources:

  • Interest.
  • Royalties.
  • State-enterprise income.
  • Fees.
  • User charges.
  • Forest receipts.
  • Irrigation receipts.

82. Federal Revenue Memory Chain

  • Tax devolution → Union taxes shared with States.
  • Vertical → Union vs States.
  • Horizontal → Among States.
  • Grants-in-aid → Transfers to States.

83. Capital Receipt Memory Chain

  • Borrowing → Liability ↑.
  • Loan recovery → Financial asset ↓.
  • Disinvestment → Government ownership ↓.

84. Tax Structure Memory Chain

  • Progressive → Burden rises with income.
  • Proportional → Same rate.
  • Regressive → Lower-income relative burden higher.

85. Tax Administration Memory Chain

  • Tax base → What is taxed.
  • Tax rate → Rate applied.
  • Buoyancy → Includes policy change.
  • Elasticity → Excludes policy change.
  • Evasion → Illegal.
  • Avoidance → Legal arrangement.
  • Compliance → Correct filing and payment.

86. TNPSC Traps

  • Government receipts are broader than revenue receipts.
  • Revenue receipts and capital receipts are different.
  • Borrowing is a capital receipt.
  • Borrowing is neither tax revenue nor non-tax revenue.
  • Tax revenue + non-tax revenue = revenue receipts.
  • Revenue receipts generally do not create liabilities.
  • Capital receipts can create liabilities or reduce assets.
  • Income tax is a direct tax.
  • Corporation tax is a direct tax.
  • GST is an indirect tax.
  • Customs duty is an indirect tax.
  • Direct-tax burden generally remains on the taxpayer.
  • Indirect-tax burden can be shifted through prices.
  • SGST relates to intra-State taxable supplies.
  • State excise is an important State revenue source.
  • Motor vehicle taxation is mainly associated with States.
  • Stamp and registration revenues are important State sources.
  • Interest and dividends are non-tax revenue.
  • Royalties are non-tax revenue.
  • Royalty means payment for use or extraction of a resource.
  • Tax and fee are different.
  • Fine is primarily punitive.
  • User charge is linked to use of a service.
  • Grant does not create a loan-repayment obligation.
  • Borrowing creates a liability.
  • Loan recovery reduces a financial asset.
  • Disinvestment reduces government ownership.
  • Vertical devolution means Union vs States.
  • Horizontal distribution means among States.
  • Cess is generally linked to a specified purpose.
  • Surcharge is an additional charge on an existing tax.
  • Horizontal equity means similar taxpayers receive similar treatment.
  • Vertical equity relates burden to ability to pay.
  • Progressive, proportional and regressive taxes are different.
  • Tax base and tax rate are different.
  • Tax buoyancy includes policy changes.
  • Tax elasticity excludes policy changes.
  • Tax evasion is illegal.
  • Avoidance and evasion are not identical.
  • Better compliance can raise revenue without higher rates.
  • Tax-GDP ratio measures tax revenue relative to GDP.
  • Higher tax-GDP ratio alone does not prove fairness or efficiency.

87. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Receipts → Revenue + Capital.
  • Revenue → Tax + Non-Tax.
  • Capital → Borrowing + Recovery + Disinvestment.
  • Direct → Income + Corporation.
  • Indirect → GST + Customs.
  • SGST → State.
  • State Excise → State.
  • Dividend → Non-Tax.
  • Interest → Non-Tax.
  • Royalty → Non-Tax.
  • Borrowing → Liability.
  • Loan Recovery → Asset ↓.
  • Disinvestment → Ownership ↓.
  • Vertical → Union–States.
  • Horizontal → Among States.
  • Cess → Specific Purpose.
  • Surcharge → Additional Tax Charge.
  • Progressive → Higher Income, Higher Relative Burden.
  • Proportional → Same Rate.
  • Regressive → Lower-Income Relative Burden Higher.
  • Evasion → Illegal.
  • Buoyancy → Includes Policy.
  • Elasticity → Excludes Policy.
  • Tax-GDP → Tax Mobilisation Capacity.

88. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Government receipts are classified into? → Revenue receipts and capital receipts.
  • Revenue receipts generally create liability? → No.
  • Revenue receipts generally reduce assets? → No.
  • Revenue receipts consist of? → Tax and non-tax revenue.
  • Capital receipts do what? → Create liabilities or reduce assets.
  • Borrowing belongs to? → Capital receipts.
  • Recovery of loans belongs to? → Capital receipts.
  • Disinvestment proceeds belong to? → Capital receipts.
  • Tax means? → Compulsory payment imposed under law.
  • Direct-tax examples? → Income tax and corporation tax.
  • Indirect-tax examples? → GST and customs duty.
  • GST is direct or indirect? → Indirect.
  • GST is what type of tax? → Destination-based tax on supply.
  • Income tax is? → Direct tax.
  • Corporation tax is? → Direct tax.
  • Customs duty is? → Indirect tax.
  • Can indirect-tax burden be shifted? → Yes.
  • SGST means? → State Goods and Services Tax.
  • SGST generally applies to? → Taxable intra-State supplies.
  • Important State revenue source on alcoholic liquor? → State excise.
  • Motor vehicle tax mainly belongs to? → States.
  • Stamp and registration revenue mainly accrues to? → States.
  • Interest receipts are? → Non-tax revenue.
  • Dividends received by government are? → Non-tax revenue.
  • Borrowing is non-tax revenue? → No.
  • Royalty means? → Payment for right to use or extract a resource.
  • Fee means? → Charge linked to specific service or regulatory activity.
  • Fine means? → Penalty for violation.
  • User charge means? → Payment by beneficiary for a specified service.
  • Grant means? → Transfer without loan repayment obligation.
  • Borrowing creates? → Liability.
  • Loan recovery reduces? → Government financial asset.
  • Disinvestment reduces? → Government ownership.
  • Tax devolution means? → Sharing divisible Union taxes with States.
  • Finance Commission role? → Tax devolution and specified grants.
  • Vertical devolution means? → Union vs States.
  • Horizontal distribution means? → Among individual States.
  • Cess means? → Tax or levy generally linked to a specified purpose.
  • Surcharge means? → Additional charge on an existing tax.
  • Horizontal equity means? → Similar taxpayers treated similarly.
  • Vertical equity means? → Greater ability to pay can bear greater burden.
  • Progressive tax? → Relative burden rises with income.
  • Proportional tax? → Same rate.
  • Regressive tax? → Relatively heavier burden on lower incomes.
  • Tax base? → Amount or activity on which tax is calculated.
  • Tax rate? → Rate applied to tax base.
  • Tax buoyancy? → Revenue response including policy changes.
  • Tax elasticity? → Revenue response excluding discretionary policy changes.
  • Tax evasion? → Illegal.
  • Tax avoidance? → Legal arrangement to reduce liability, subject to anti-avoidance rules.
  • Tax compliance? → Correct registration, reporting, filing and payment.
  • Digitalisation improves? → Tax administration and compliance.
  • Tax-GDP ratio measures? → Tax revenue relative to GDP.
  • Rising tax-GDP ratio can provide? → Greater fiscal space.
